justice: A paved sidewalk is present along the left side of the street, so pedestrian space is provided rather than forcing all users into the carriageway.
Spatial resources are unevenly distributed because the right side is dominated by surface parking spaces and parked cars, while a clear pedestrian path is not visible there.
Accessibility is only moderate because the visible sidewalk appears smooth and relatively wide, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossing facilities can be identified in the image.
safety: The roadway is straight with a centerline and directional arrows, which helps drivers understand movement and reduces confusion.
Safety is weakened by parked cars directly along the right edge of the travel lane, creating potential dooring and visibility conflicts for pedestrians and cyclists.
Streetlights are visible and the road surface is well maintained, but there is no visible protected bike lane, crosswalk, or strong traffic-calming feature.
livability: The street appears clean and orderly, with maintained planting strips, trees, and a formal building frontage contributing to a decent everyday environment.
Livability is limited because the scene shows few active uses at street level; the long blank institutional or commercial facade offers little social interaction or small-scale street life.
No benches, outdoor seating, kiosks for public use, or visible gathering spaces are present, reducing opportunities for lingering and community activity.
sustainability: The tree line on the right side provides meaningful green coverage and some ecological value compared with a fully hardscaped corridor.
Permeable or semi-permeable grass parking strips are visible under some parked cars, which may support rainwater infiltration better than full asphalt paving.
Sustainability is reduced by the large amount of land devoted to private car parking and the absence of visible cycling infrastructure or public transit facilities.
aesthetics: The street has a neat and coherent visual order, with a uniform road section, consistent lighting poles, and organized parking.
A continuous row of mature trees and flowering vegetation on the right softens the corridor and improves visual quality.
Aesthetics are somewhat weakened by the long, monotonous facade of the large building on the left and the strong visual presence of parked vehicles.
comfort: Physical comfort is moderate because the left sidewalk appears smooth, level, and unobstructed for walking.
Thermal comfort is mixed: the right side benefits from substantial tree cover, but the left sidewalk beside the large building appears exposed to sun with little visible shade.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the broad expanse of asphalt, sparse human presence, and parking-dominated edge, which can make the street feel less welcoming for non-drivers.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk is visible on the left side, and its surface appears even enough for routine walking.
Walkability is limited because there is no visible crosswalk, curb extension, or clear pedestrian priority treatment across the street.
The long inactive facade on the left and the parking edge on the right make the route functional but not especially engaging or pedestrian-oriented.
bikeability: There is no visible dedicated bike lane, painted bicycle marking, or protected cycling space anywhere along the corridor.
Parked cars along the right side create potential conflicts for cyclists from opening doors and vehicles entering or leaving parking spaces.
The straight, relatively low-complexity roadway may be rideable for confident cyclists, but the lack of separation and bicycle facilities keeps overall bikeability low.
